title: Evidence-based practice, research and critical thinking
blurb: Rank evidence, tell research from audit and service evaluation, and apply guidance with professional judgement.
question: A ward wants to check whether its nurses are documenting falls risk assessments within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires. Is this research, audit or service evaluation, and does it need research ethics committee review?

teach.body: Evidence-based practice combines the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the person's own values and preferences. Code 6.1 requires that any information or advice you give is evidence-based, and 6.2 that you maintain the knowledge and skills you need. Plain English: do things because good evidence shows they work and they suit this person, not because 'we've always done it this way'.

teach.caption: Based on the Oxford CEBM levels: a systematic review of RCTs is level 1a; expert opinion is level 5.
Health Research Authority, Defining research table (October 2022).

teach.body: NICE guidance is not mandatory. Professionals are expected to take it fully into account when exercising their judgement, alongside the individual needs, preferences and values of the person. So you follow guidance as the default, but you think critically about whether it fits this person, and you document and discuss any reasoned departure from it.

teach.caption: Your experience and clinical judgement bring the evidence and the person together.

items: Is the question clear and relevant to your patients?
Is the design suited to the question (for example an RCT for a treatment)?
How large and representative was the sample? Could bias explain the result?
Were participants' consent and ethics approval in place?
Do the results apply to the person in front of you?

teach.h: Worked scenario: Charge Nurse Ruth on an elderly care ward
teach.body: Ruth wants to know whether falls risk assessments are being completed within 6 hours, as trust policy requires. She is measuring practice against a set standard, with no new intervention or randomisation, so this is clinical audit and does not need NHS research ethics review. If she instead compared two new types of sensor alarm by randomly allocating patients, that would be research needing ethics approval.

teach.text: AUDIT measures against a STANDARD; SERVICE EVALUATION describes current care with NO standard; RESEARCH creates NEW, generalisable knowledge and normally needs NHS REC review. Randomising patients is a sign of research.

items: Code 6.1: information and advice must be evidence-based.
Systematic reviews of RCTs sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy; expert opinion at the bottom.
NICE guidance is not mandatory: apply it with judgement and the person's preferences.
Research needs NHS REC review; audit and service evaluation normally do not.

summary: You can now rank types of evidence, distinguish research from audit and service evaluation, and say which needs ethics review. You can also explain how to apply guidance with professional judgement and appraise a study critically.

A.q: Which type of evidence sits at the top of the hierarchy for questions about treatment effectiveness?
A.why: A systematic review of randomised controlled trials is level 1a in the Oxford CEBM levels of evidence for treatment.

whyNot.0: Cohort studies rank below RCTs and systematic reviews of RCTs.
whyNot.1: Expert opinion is the lowest level (level 5).
whyNot.3: Case series rank low because they have no comparison group.

A.q: A team measures how many patients received pain reassessment within 30 minutes of analgesia against the trust standard. What is this?
A.why: Clinical audit measures current care against a predetermined standard (HRA Defining research table).

whyNot.0: Research generates new, generalisable knowledge, often testing a hypothesis.
whyNot.2: Service evaluation measures current care without reference to a standard.
whyNot.3: Health surveillance monitors threats to population health, such as outbreaks.

A.q: What is the status of NICE guidance for a registered nurse?
options: It is a legal requirement in every case
It applies to doctors rather than nurses
It is optional and may be set aside freely
It must be fully considered with judgement
A.why: NICE guidance is not mandatory; professionals are expected to take it fully into account alongside the individual needs and preferences of the person.

whyNot.0: NICE guidance is not a legal requirement.
whyNot.1: NICE guidance applies to all healthcare professionals.
whyNot.2: It is not mandatory, but it cannot be ignored: it must be taken fully into account.

B.q: A nurse plans to randomly allocate patients to two different dressings to see which heals leg ulcers faster. What does this project need before starting?
options: Approval from the ward's audit lead
Verbal agreement from the ward manager
B.why: Allocating patients to interventions to produce generalisable findings is research, which normally needs NHS research ethics committee review (HRA).

whyNot.1: This is not audit, so audit approval is not enough.
whyNot.2: A manager's agreement does not replace ethics review for research.
whyNot.3: It is not a service evaluation, as it involves allocation to treatments.

B.q: A ward asks patients about their experience of the new discharge lounge. No standard is being compared. What type of project is this?
B.why: Service evaluation measures what the current service achieves without reference to a standard (HRA).

whyNot.0: No new generalisable knowledge or hypothesis is being tested.
whyNot.1: Audit compares against a set standard, which is absent here.
whyNot.2: No one is being randomly allocated.

B.q: A NICE guideline recommends a treatment, but a patient with capacity prefers a different evidence-based option. What should the nurse do?
options: Discuss the options and support an informed choice
Refer the patient for a capacity assessment
Withhold treatment until the patient agrees
B.why: Guidance is applied with professional judgement and the person's preferences (NICE 'Your responsibility'; Code 2.3).

whyNot.0: NICE guidance does not override the choice of a person with capacity.
whyNot.2: Preferring another option is not a reason to doubt capacity.
whyNot.3: Withholding treatment to force agreement is coercive.

C.q: A nurse reads a small study of 12 patients from one hospital showing a new mouthwash prevents pneumonia. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Dismiss it, as small studies are worthless
Appraise it critically and look for stronger evidence
Ask patients whether they would like to try it
C.why: Critical appraisal considers sample size, bias and applicability. A small single-site study is weak evidence, so look for systematic reviews or guidance before changing practice (P1.7, P1.8).

whyNot.0: Changing practice on weak evidence may cause harm.
whyNot.1: Small studies can be useful but need cautious interpretation.
whyNot.3: Offering an unproven treatment without stronger evidence is not evidence-based (Code 6.1).

C.q: A nurse re-audits fluid balance chart completion six months after introducing a new chart. Which stage of the audit cycle is she completing?
options: Re-audit to check change has worked
C.why: Re-audit closes the audit loop by checking whether changes have improved practice against the standard.

whyNot.1: The standard was set before the first audit.
whyNot.2: Baseline data came from the first audit.
whyNot.3: The topic was chosen at the start of the cycle.

C.q: A patient asks a nurse about a herbal supplement for her arthritis that she saw advertised online. What does Code 6.1 require?
options: Recommend it if other patients report benefit
Avoid discussing products she has not tried
Tell her to follow the advert's advice
Give advice based on the best available evidence
C.why: Code 6.1: make sure any information or advice given is evidence-based, including information about using health and care products.

whyNot.1: Personal experience of a product is not the standard; evidence is.

reteach.title: Three questions to sort any project
reteach.question: Is it new knowledge, a check against a standard, or a description of what happens now?

blocks.h: Ask what the project is trying to find out
blocks.body: If it asks 'what is best?' and could apply elsewhere, it is RESEARCH. If it asks 'are we meeting the standard?', it is AUDIT. If it asks 'what does our service achieve?', it is SERVICE EVALUATION. Randomly allocating people to treatments points to research, which normally needs ethics review.

blocks.text: Patient satisfaction surveys are usually SERVICE EVALUATION, not research, unless they test a hypothesis for generalisable knowledge.

explain.body: For treatment: systematic review of RCTs, then RCTs, cohort, case-control, case series, expert opinion.

test.q: Which study design ranks lowest in the hierarchy for treatment questions?
test.why: Expert opinion without critical appraisal is the lowest level (level 5) in the CEBM hierarchy.

whyNot.0: Cohort studies rank above case-control and expert opinion.
whyNot.3: Case-control studies rank above expert opinion.

explain.body: Planned to produce generalisable or transferable findings, may test a hypothesis or randomise participants, normally needs NHS REC review.

test.q: Which feature most clearly identifies a project as research rather than audit?
options: It aims at generalisable new knowledge
It collects data from clinical records
It is led by a senior registered nurse
It produces a written report for the board
test.why: The HRA defines research by its aim to derive generalisable or transferable new knowledge.

whyNot.2: Nurses lead audits as well as research.

explain.body: Measures current practice against a set standard, then changes practice and re-audits.

test.q: What is the defining feature of clinical audit?
test.why: Audit measures practice against a predetermined, recognised standard.

whyNot.0: Random allocation is a feature of research.
whyNot.3: Measuring without a standard is service evaluation.

explain.body: NICE guidance is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account, alongside the person's needs and preferences.

test.q: Which Code standard requires nurses to maintain the knowledge and skills needed for safe and effective practice?
test.why: Code 6.2: maintain the knowledge and skills you need for safe and effective practice.

whyNot.0: 6.1 is about evidence-based information and advice.
whyNot.1: 9.4 is about supporting students' and colleagues' learning.
whyNot.2: 10.6 is about collecting and storing data and research findings.
